newsitem.title: FRANCE: French far-rightist Le Pen on sale in many forms.
newsitem.headline: French far-rightist Le Pen on sale in many forms.

text.p: Delegates to France's far-right National Front congress can buy Jean-Marie Le Pen's image emblazoned on a cigarette lighter, painted on a wooden plaque or smiling from a TV screen via a videocassette.
But the most popular stand at the Front's three-day meeting in Strasbourg, eastern France, was easily the booth selling local Alsatian wine and pastry.
The Strasbourg convention centre's official food stands sold only sandwiches, and delegates -- restricted to the centre for security reasons -- quickly tired of ham or salami on a baguette.
Party officials insisted sales were brisk in Le Pen videos and tracts.
But the lines in front of the Alsace stand built up early in the morning and never got shorter.
Strasbourg is celebrated for its heavy Germanic fare, especially sausages, sauerkraut and potatoes.

The Front's burly security guards cautioned delegates against roaming the city centre so as to avoid clashes with anti-Front protesters who poured into Strasbourg to flaunt their opposition to the party's growing political influence.

So instead of sampling the delights of the city, delegates were left to buy tapes and cassettes of French martial music, watch a video of "The Front - The Hope: Images of 1996" or be briefed on the Front's new site on the global Internet computer network (HTTP://WWW.FRONT-NAT.FR).
Also on sale were rolls of brightly coloured stickers to help spread the Front's ideas.
A roll of stickers reading "Shoot (drug) dealers" or "Expel illegal immigrants" was priced at 150 francs ($26).
"Sales are great," said a man running the sticker booth. He said all proceeds from the sale of party books, pamphlets and posters were ploughed back into the party to help it spread the word.
Were it not for the security guards and the unusual merchandise, the meeting could easily have masqueraded as a convention of shopkeepers or postal workers.
Nowhere were skinheads or swastikas in evidence.
Party leaders worked hard to put a mainstream gloss on their congress, with dramatic lighting, loud music (although no rock and roll) and a cocktail party for the media.
